etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from French révolter, from Italian rivoltare, itself either from ri- with the verb voltare, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *revoltāre < *revolvitāre, for *revolūtāre, frequentative of Latin revolvō (“roll back”) (through its past participle revolūtus).

quote.citation: c. 1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life and Death of King Iohn”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i], page 18, column 1:

1796–1797, Edmund Burke, “Letters on a Regicide Peace, Continued from Vol. VIII. Letter IV. To the Earl Fitzwilliam.”, in [Walker King], editor, The Works of the Right Honourable Edmund Burke, new edition, volume IX, London:  […]  [R. Gilbert] for C[harles] and J[ohn] Rivington, […], published 1826, →OCLC, page 118:
quote.text: I shall be told, that this abominable medley is made rather to revolt young and ingenuous minds.

quote.citation: 1870, John Morley, Condorcet (published in the Fortnightly Review
quote.text: To derive delight from what inflicts pain on any sentient creature revolted his conscience and offended his reason.

definitions.definition: To cause to turn back; to roll or drive back; to put to flight.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book III, Canto XI”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, page 567:
quote.text: The foring clouds into fad fhowres y molt; / So to her yold the flames, and did their force reuolt.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be disgusted, shocked, or grossly offended; hence, to feel nausea; used with at.
To turn away; to abandon or reject something; specifically, to turn away, or shrink, with abhorrence.

quote.citation: 1673, John Milton, “[Sonnet] XII. On the Same [Tetrachordon].”, in Poems, &c. upon Several Occasions, London:  […]  Tho[mas] Dring […], →OCLC, page 57:
quote.text: And ſtill revolt when truth would ſet them free.

quote.citation: 1886, John Morley, The Life of Turgot:
quote.text: His clear intelligence revolted from the dominant sophisms of that time.
